title: Simple attention
hook: a cook, a reformer and a poet agree: prayer can be mostly looking

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary in Carmel, the order's mother and its sister. Your line was sister and mother. Did you walk alongside someone instead of advising from above? Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

"Be still and see that I am God." That's the psalm, in the Douay-Rheims. Notice the verbs. Not speak. Not ask. Not explain. Be still, and see. Prayer often means talking, and talking is good. But over these weeks in Carmel, a different kind has kept surfacing underneath the stories: the hermit's cell, Teresa's friend, John's night, Elizabeth's inner room. Strip them back, and what's left is something very plain. Today, simple attention.
screen: `BE STILL, AND SEE.` → `NOT SPEAK, NOT ASK.` → `WHAT'S LEFT UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: First, Teresa. In The Way of Perfection, writing to her sisters, she says she isn't asking them for long reflections or clever thoughts about God. She asks only that they look at him. Just look. If you're tired or sad, she says, look at him tired and sad in the gospel, and he will look back at you. Second, John of the Cross. John says that when meditation dries up, a person shouldn't panic and force more thinking. They can rest in what he calls a loving attention to God, quiet and peaceful, not doing much at all. That isn't laziness, he says. It's letting God do the work. Third, the cook. Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection was a Carmelite lay brother in Paris who spent years in the monastery kitchen. His letters and conversations were gathered after his death. He describes keeping himself in God's presence by a simple attention and a loving gaze, in the clatter of the kitchen just as in chapel. For him, turning an omelet could be prayer. Fourth, what it isn't. Simple attention doesn't mean emptying the mind, or forcing a feeling. It means noticing God the way you'd notice someone you love across a room: warmly, without a speech. Teresa, John and Brother Lawrence lived different lives, a reformer, a poet, a cook. Yet the prayer underneath sounds the same in all three. Carmel, at its plainest, is someone looking at God with love, and letting that be enough.
screen: `TERESA: ONLY LOOK AT HIM.` · `JOHN: A LOVING ATTENTION.` · `LAWRENCE: GOD IN THE KITCHEN.` · then, large: `BE STILL AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: attend to God, simply, for five minutes. The bell gives us the first two. Settle, and breathe. Don't plan anything to say. Just turn your attention, gently, toward God, the way you'd glance at someone you love who's reading in the same room. When thoughts come, and they will, don't fight them. Notice, and turn back. If you pray, you can let one word carry the attention, a name, or just: here. If you don't, simply rest your attention on the breath, warmly, and stay. After the bell, try three minutes more. The bell holds the time.
Simple attention. Carmel's plainest prayer: looking at God with love, without a speech. Today's word.

Your line: loving attention. Today, pick one ordinary chore, the dishes, the laundry, the drive, and do it the way Brother Lawrence did, attending to God in the middle of it. Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Carmelites keep times of silent prayer each day in which they rest in loving attention to God, and some Catholics practice Brother Lawrence's habit of turning to God in the middle of ordinary work.

fork.setup: you've prayed with thoughts and words for years, and now they've dried up. sitting down to pray feels empty. what does John of the Cross suggest?
options: force more thinking until the feeling returns.
rest in a quiet, loving attention to God.
fork.reveal: John says not to panic and force it, but to rest in loving attention, letting God do the work.

trapdoor: what you thought: real prayer needs lots of words.
what it means: in Carmel, prayer can be mostly loving attention, looking at God and letting that be enough.
what a scholar hears: Teresa's Way of Perfection 26, John's loving attention in the Ascent and the Living Flame, and Brother Lawrence's practice of the presence of God.

notes: Teresa, Way of Perfection 26 paraphrased ('I'm only asking you to look at him'; look at him sad or tired as he is in the Gospel). Confirm chapter and paraphrase.
John of the Cross on 'loving attention' when meditation fails: paraphrased; confirm references (Ascent 2.12–15; Living Flame 3).

Brother Lawrence: Discalced Carmelite lay brother in Paris, kitchen work; 'simple attention and a loving gaze' paraphrased (the 1890s English versions read close to 'simple attention, and a general fond regard to God'); the omelet detail is from his conversations. Confirm.
Outline practice is five minutes; the app sit is two, so the practice invites three more after the bell.
